group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 67-year-old man presented this afternoon to the ambulatory perioperative medicine service for evaluation four days before a planned elective laparoscopic ventral incisional hernia repair with composite mesh; the general surgery team anticipates three trocar sites plus a 2-cm periumbilical assist incision, approximately 90 minutes of operative time under general anesthesia, blood loss under 100 mL, same-day admission to the surgical ward, and discharge on postoperative day 1 once oral intake, pain control, and ambulation criteria are met. He arrived by city bus, walked from the stop at the far end of the medical center grounds, ascended one flight of stairs rather than using the elevator, and conversed comfortably with staff without need to pause. At home he mows his small yard with a push mower, walks his dog on a half-mile loop that includes a modest hill, and carries a 16-pound granddaughter up a flight of stairs without chest tightness, dyspnea, or palpitations, though he notes having to slow his pace slightly near the top. Five and a half years ago he was hospitalized for abrupt heavy pressure in the mid-sternum associated with diaphoresis while shoveling wet snow; emergency coronary angiography at that time revealed a 95 % proximal left anterior descending lesion for which a drug-eluting stent was deployed, peak troponin I reached 8 ng/mL, and he completed a phase-II cardiac rehabilitation program without residual angina. He follows cardiology every six months, and a bicycle stress echocardiogram performed eight months ago achieved 9 metabolic equivalents with no inducible wall-motion abnormalities. Current cardiovascular medications include aspirin 81 mg every morning, metoprolol succinate 25 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and lisinopril 10 mg at breakfast; pharmacy refill history and his own pill organizer support excellent adherence. Long-standing essential hypertension is controlled on this regimen with home readings averaging 122–128/70–74 mm Hg. He denies any history of stroke, transient neurologic deficits, carotid procedures, atrial fibrillation, peripheral artery disease, congestive symptoms such as orthopnea or lower-extremity swelling, syncope, or implantable cardiac devices. Chronic kidney disease was first noted three years ago during an annual wellness visit when creatinine exceeded 1.6 mg/dL; repeat measurements have been stable in the 1.7–1.9 mg/dL range, and urinalysis consistently shows only trace protein without hematuria. He has never been told he has diabetes; fasting glucose values drawn by his primary-care physician run in the 90–110 mg/dL range, and the most recent hemoglobin A1c was 5.6 %. Pulmonary history is limited to mild seasonal allergic rhinitis relieved with intranasal fluticasone; he quit cigarette smoking 18 years ago after a 12-pack-year exposure and now drinks one 12-ounce beer with Sunday dinner, denying illicit drug use entirely. Prior operations include an open appendectomy at age 28 and cataract extraction of the right eye at 63 without anesthetic complications. Family history reveals a father who died of myocardial infarction at 72 and a mother living with osteoporosis; no first-degree relatives experienced cerebrovascular events before age 75. Review of systems today is negative for fever, cough, wheeze at rest, exertional paroxysms, orthostatic dizziness, claudication, abdominal pain beyond the reducible midline bulge, dyspepsia, urinary changes, or unintentional weight loss. After five minutes of seated rest, vital signs obtained in the left arm showed blood pressure 124/72 mm Hg, regular radial pulse 64 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 97 % on room air, and oral temperature 36.6 °C; he stands 178 cm tall, weighs 86 kg, and has a body-mass index of 27.1 kg/m². He appears well nourished, in no distress, and euvolemic. Neck veins are not distended at 45°, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse is localized in the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line, normal in amplitude and duration. Heart sounds reveal a crisp S1, physiologic splitting of S2, and no gallop, click, or murmur. Lungs are clear to percussion and auscultation with full diaphragmatic excursion. Abdomen shows a 4-cm midline fascial defect superior to a healed peri-umbilical scar that becomes more prominent with Valsalva; there is no tenderness, guarding, or organomegaly, and bowel sounds are active. Extremities are warm with 2+ dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally, no edema, and good capillary refill. Cranial nerves II-XII are intact, strength is 5/5 throughout, sensation is preserved to light touch and vibration, and tandem gait is steady. Airway evaluation by the anesthesia nurse reveals Mallampati class I view, inter-incisor distance 4 cm, thyromental distance 6.5 cm, full cervical extension, and stable dentition. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn one hour before examination demonstrate hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, platelet count 258 × 10⁹/L, white blood cells 6.0 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 29 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 1.88 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of approximately 43 mL/min/1.73 m²; fasting glucose obtained simultaneously is 102 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 26 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 24 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 90 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.0. A 12-lead electrocardiogram recorded today shows normal sinus rhythm at 66 beats/min, PR interval 160 ms, QRS duration 94 ms, axis 45°, and inferior Q waves with anterior T-wave inversions unchanged from a tracing six months earlier; no acute ST-segment deviations or new conduction abnormalities are present. Upright postero-anterior chest radiography demonstrates a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette, clear lung fields, and intact diaphragm contours. The perioperative plan, reviewed with the patient and documented in the chart, is to continue aspirin and beta-blocker on the morning of surgery, postpone lisinopril until he has resumed oral intake, employ lung-protective ventilation with moderate positive end-expiratory pressure, insert a radial arterial line only if intraoperative hemodynamic instability arises, administer goal-directed crystalloid guided by pulse pressure variation to avoid fluid overload in the setting of reduced renal reserve, and begin early ambulation with incentive spirometry within six hours of arrival to the ward. The patient provided accurate teach-back regarding midnight fasting, medication timing, wound-care expectations, and signs of myocardial ischemia or acute kidney injury that would warrant prompt reporting, and he voiced understanding as well as willingness to proceed with hernia repair later this week.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) assigns 1 point for each of six preoperative factors:
- High-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, or suprainguinal vascular): 0 if the planned ventral hernia repair is classified as an abdominal-wall procedure rather than an intraperitoneal operation. This distinction matters: an intraperitoneal approach would add 1 under the original RCRI definition.
- Ischemic heart disease: 1. The prior MI with LAD stenting qualifies despite good current exercise tolerance and a negative stress test.
- Congestive heart failure: 0; no history or clinical signs.
- Cerebrovascular disease: 0; no stroke or TIA.
- Diabetes treated with insulin: 0; he does not have diabetes.
- Preoperative creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: 0; creatinine is 1.88 mg/dL. Reduced eGFR does not itself score.
With the abdominal-wall classification, the sum is 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 1.
Final answer: 1
